headline: Bedrocan trustees' report backs founder before 26 November debate
dek: Bedrocan's court-appointed trustees say the Dutch cannabis agency's refusal to take ordered stock led to bankruptcy, ahead of a 26 November debate.
key_points: The trustees' first public report, filed on 9 November, names the state cannabis agency's refusal to take delivery of stock it ordered from 2023 as the root cause, Business of Cannabis reported.
Bedrocan Nederland was profitable: revenue of €20.5 million and operating profit of €2.58 million in 2025, and €12.49 million and €1.91 million in the first nine months of 2026.
Founder Tjalling Erkelens sent MPs an 11-page rebuttal on 16 November with 13 questions for Health Minister Sophie Hermans.
The Dutch House of Representatives debates the collapse on 26 November; a restart bid awaits a judge's approval and the bidder is not named.
body: A week before the Dutch parliament debates the collapse of Bedrocan, the public record has shifted against the government's version of events. Business of Cannabis published a three-part examination on 19 November of the three accounts now on file: the health minister's, the founder's and that of the court-appointed trustees. On the central question of what caused the bankruptcy, the trustees' report lines up with the founder.

Bedrocan Nederland B.V. was for two decades the only domestic producer of medical cannabis in the Netherlands, selling its whole output to the state's Bureau voor Medicinale Cannabis (BMC). It went bankrupt in October. The Tweede Kamer, the House of Representatives, is due to debate the case on 26 November. As we reported on 11 November, Health Minister Sophie Hermans has told MPs that a European tender for a replacement supplier will be published in December.
## The minister's account

In her letter of 6 November, Hermans called the bankruptcy a regrettable development and a matter of ordinary business risk. She wrote that the state's service agreement with Bedrocan ended on 1 January 2026 and that the company's later difficulties were therefore not the result of that termination, according to Business of Cannabis.

During the suspension of payments that came before bankruptcy, she wrote, the administrator asked the state to help, for example by paying invoices before quality checks were finished. The state's lawyer advised against it and the cabinet declined, citing the risk of paying for unusable cannabis and doubt that a restart would succeed. After bankruptcy the state chose not to take over the remaining stock, saying it already held enough of the Bedrocan variety for Dutch demand.
## The trustees' account

The trustees, Arno Gras and Floris Verduijn, filed their first public bankruptcy report with the Noord-Nederland district court on 9 November. Their job is to get the most for creditors and judge whether a restart is viable, which is why Business of Cannabis treats their report as the most neutral of the three.

According to the outlet, the report describes the contract between Bedrocan and the BMC as a framework agreement to buy and supply medical cannabis, not a service agreement. It identifies the BMC's refusal to take delivery of stock it had ordered from 2023 onward as the underlying cause of the insolvency. The so-called freezer incident of September 2023, when inspectors found far more batches in storage than permitted, appears in the report as a result of that commercial failure, not its cause.

The report also records that Rabobank, Bedrocan's main secured lender, was willing to finance a restructuring if the BMC guaranteed full payment for batches it had ordered and that had passed quality control. The BMC said the batches were not needed for its statutory task and did not cooperate with other buyers the trustees proposed. On 7 October the trustees asked the court to convert the suspension of payments into bankruptcy. All 69 employees were dismissed the next day.
> The trustees have no side in the political fight, and their figures describe a profitable grower with one customer that stopped collecting.
## The numbers

The financial figures cut against the picture of a failing business. Bedrocan Nederland's revenue was €19.94 million in 2024, €20.50 million in 2025 and €12.49 million in the first nine months of 2026, the report says. Operating profit (EBIT) was €1.35 million, €2.58 million and €1.91 million over the same periods. On our calculation that is an operating margin of about 12.6% in 2025 and about 15.3% in 2026 to September.

At bankruptcy the company held 340 kg of finished product and 390 kg in cultivation under the main state supply regime, about 730 kg in all, plus 250 kg grown under a second regime for extract makers. After the bankruptcy, the BMC agreed to take delivery of batches it had earlier declined to pay for and to resell them to a buyer found by Bedrocan's commercial team, Business of Cannabis reported.
## The founder's rebuttal

Founder and former chairman Tjalling Erkelens sent an 11-page rebuttal to parliament's health committee on 16 November, with 13 proposed questions for the minister and a draft motion. He says the BMC ordered 3,890 kg across 69 batches in October 2022 and February 2023, expecting German demand to grow after export limits were lifted, and then could not sell it. By the September 2023 inspection, he says, 37 batches sat in Bedrocan's freezers at Emmeloord against a contractual maximum of two, and they were the BMC's uncollected orders.

Erkelens says the two sides signed a confidential settlement agreement in November 2025 covering 2026, which the minister's letter does not mention, and he wants parliament to compel its disclosure. He says the BMC refused in mid-September 2026 to pay an invoice of about €345,000 three weeks early and then withheld two more totalling about €372,000 for approved product. That is roughly €717,000, on our sum. The minister described the request as payment for untested cannabis; Erkelens says the product had passed. He calls the state's conduct "deliberate administrative sabotage", Business of Cannabis reported. These are his claims, and the ministry has not accepted them.
He also says the BMC on 13 November rejected a joint application by Bedrocan and the Dutch manufacturer Cannadis Europe for 250 to 500 kg of flower for extraction.
## What it means for patients and buyers

The supply clock has not changed. The minister's letter puts the last deliveries of Bedrobinol in early Q2 2027, Bedrolite in early Q3 and the Bedrocan, Bediol and Bedica varieties in mid-Q3. She says no effect on availability is expected for now but concedes patients will probably have to switch products at some point. Erkelens disputes that switching is safe for some patients, citing Dutch medicines-board advice against switching in treatment-resistant epilepsy.

For the United Kingdom, where Bedrolite is used to make oil for children with severe epilepsy, the minister says an investigation is under way into supplying it a little longer. The trustees describe their chosen restart as the best route to keep supplying the Netherlands and export markets including the UK, Germany, Italy and Finland. Separately, the group's Canadian shares and intellectual property have been sold to Becanex for €200,000, subject to the judge's confirmation.

For importers and pharmacies that relied on Bedrocan flower, the practical point is that a restart is possible but unfunded in public view, and the tender timetable does not deliver new supply before stocks run down.
## What to watch

Watch the Tweede Kamer debate on 26 November, and whether MPs demand the 2025 settlement agreement. Watch for the supervisory judge's decision on the restart bid and the identity of the bidder. The European tender is due in December 2026, with a supplier to be chosen in May 2027. The minister has promised an update on the tender and the delayed Opium Act amendment in spring 2027.
